summary: Defines the Proxy-Status HTTP response header field, which lets an intermediary report details of how it handled a response, including errors it generated. This helps people tell whether a problem came from the proxy or the origin server. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A middleman writes a note saying what went wrong when a package could not be delivered.

questions: how to debug proxy errors in http
what does proxy-status error connection_timeout mean
subtitle: A response header that lets proxies and CDNs say what they did and what went wrong on the way to the origin.

tldr.problem: When a proxy or CDN generates an error such as 502 or 504, the status code alone says too little about what really happened, which makes debugging hard.
tldr.mechanism: Each intermediary adds a member to a Proxy-Status response field, with parameters such as error, next-hop, next-protocol, received-status and details, and the RFC defines 32 proxy error types.
tldr.outcome: Clients and operators can tell whether a failure came from the proxy or the origin, though the content is unverified and can leak internal details if used carelessly.

today: RFC 9209 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the Proxy-Status field and the two IANA registries for its parameters and error types.

sections.title: Why Intermediaries Need to Explain Themselves
sections.content:
HTTP intermediaries, both forward proxies and gateways (also called reverse proxies), are a significant part of HTTP deployments. Reverse proxies and content delivery networks (CDNs) form part of the critical infrastructure of many websites.

Normally an intermediary forwards a request toward the origin server and forwards the response back. If an error happens before a response is obtained, the intermediary often generates the response itself. HTTP has a few status codes for this, such as 502 (Bad Gateway) and 504 (Gateway Timeout), but experience has shown that more information is needed to aid debugging. RFC 9209 defines the Proxy-Status response field so that intermediaries can describe how they handled a response.
sections.eli5: When a parcel gets lost, "it did not arrive" is not much help. Proxy-Status is the delivery person's note that says where and why.

sections.title: The Proxy-Status Field
sections.content:
The value of Proxy-Status is a Structured Field List. Each member represents one intermediary that handled the response. The first member is the one closest to the origin server, and the last is the one closest to the user agent. For example, Proxy-Status: revproxy1.example.net, ExampleCDN means the response went through revproxy1.example.net first and then ExampleCDN.

Each member MUST be a String or a Token that identifies the intermediary. It can be a service name ("ExampleCDN" is fine, but a product name such as "ExampleProxy" is not, because it does not identify the deployment), a hostname, an IP address or a generated string. Parameters on a member are all optional, and unrecognised parameters MUST be ignored.

Intermediaries decide when to add the field. Some add it to every response; others only when configured to, or when a request header turns on a debugging mode. They SHOULD keep existing members so the whole chain can be debugged, unless configured to remove them. Origin servers MUST NOT generate the field.
sections.eli5: Each helper along the road signs the note in order, so you can see everyone who touched the parcel, from the shop to your door.

sections.title: Trailers and Ordering
sections.content:
The field MAY be sent as a trailer field. This helps when a proxy is streaming a response and the inbound connection suddenly ends, since the header section has already been sent. Because trailers can be silently discarded along the path, it SHOULD NOT be sent as a trailer unless it cannot be sent in the header section.

To keep the order of members clear, an intermediary MUST NOT send Proxy-Status as a trailer unless it also sent a header field with the same member, though possibly with different parameters. A client MAY promote a trailer member into the header field by replacing the first matching header member, comparing the String or Token without parameters, and then removing the trailer if it is empty.

Example from the RFC: a proxy called ThisProxy adds itself to SomeOtherProxy to give SomeOtherProxy, ThisProxy, and can then append the trailer ThisProxy; error=read_timeout.
sections.eli5: If the proxy runs out of room on the front of the envelope, it can tuck a note in at the back, as long as the front already names it.

sections.title: The Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC defines five parameters.

  • error: a Token naming a proxy error type. It means the intermediary hit a problem getting this response. Some types mean the intermediary itself made the response; others can be added to a partial response from an inbound server, for example as a trailer when the forward connection closes abruptly.
  • next-hop: a String or Token identifying the intermediary or origin server used to get the response, such as backend.example.org:8001.
  • next-protocol: the ALPN protocol identifier used to connect to the next hop, as a Token or Byte Sequence. A Token MUST be used if the identifier can be expressed that way, for example h2.
  • received-status: an Integer holding the HTTP status code received from the next hop.
  • details: a String with extra information not captured elsewhere.

When sending error, the most specific accurate error type SHOULD be used, and the response status code SHOULD be the type's recommended code, though other codes may be used, for example when a status was already sent. A real example from the RFC: a 504 response with Proxy-Status: ExampleCDN; error=connection_timeout was generated by ExampleCDN because of a connection timeout going forward.
sections.eli5: The note has boxes to fill in: what went wrong, who was next in line, how you talked to them, what they said back, and a spot for anything else.

sections.title: Proxy Error Types
sections.content:
Section 2.3 defines 32 proxy error types. Each has a name, a description, any extra parameters, a recommended HTTP status code and a flag saying whether the response is only generated by intermediaries. Implementations might not produce every type.

They fall into groups: DNS problems (dns_timeout, dns_error); destination problems (destination_not_found, destination_unavailable, destination_ip_prohibited, destination_ip_unroutable); connection problems (connection_refused, connection_terminated, connection_timeout, read and write timeouts, connection_limit_reached); TLS problems (tls_protocol_error, tls_certificate_error, tls_alert_received); HTTP problems such as http_request_error, http_request_denied, incomplete or oversized responses, coding errors, http_response_timeout, http_upgrade_failed and http_protocol_error; and proxy-internal problems (proxy_internal_response, proxy_internal_error, proxy_configuration_error, proxy_loop_detected).

Some types carry extra parameters. For instance, dns_error has rcode and info-code, and tls_alert_received has alert-id and alert-message. The generic http_protocol_error should only be used when a more specific type is not defined.

The type http_request_error is for when the intermediary generates a 4xx response on the origin's behalf, which helps tell proxy-made responses from origin-made ones. In the RFC's example, a 429 response with error=http_request_error from r34.example.net shows it came from that proxy, not the CDN or origin.
sections.eli5: There is a list of reasons a delivery can fail, like wrong address, nobody home, or door locked. The helper picks the closest one.

sections.title: Adding New Parameters and Error Types
sections.content:
New parameters go in the "HTTP Proxy-Status Parameters" registry and new error types go in the "HTTP Proxy Error Types" registry. Both use Expert Review under RFC 8126, and a specification document is appreciated but not required.

Experts should weigh community feedback, whether the value is well defined, and a preference for generic over vendor-specific values. If no generic name can be agreed, the name should be specific, for example with a vendor prefix. Names must not clash between the two registries.
sections.eli5: If the list of reasons is missing one, anyone can ask a small panel to add it, as long as it is clear and useful.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main concern is leaking information that helps an attacker, such as details of the intermediary's configuration and backend topology. That could let attackers target backend services that are not ready for heavy traffic or malformed input.

Intermediaries are not required to generate the field or any parameter, and can do so conditionally, for example based on authentication tokens or IP address. The content is also not verified: an intermediary can claim an action, such as using an encrypted channel, without really doing it.
sections.eli5: The delivery note should not tell strangers where the back door is, so helpers choose carefully what to write and who gets to read it.

data.title: Proxy-Status examples
data.code:
Proxy-Status: revproxy1.example.net, ExampleCDN

HTTP/1.1 504 Gateway Timeout
Proxy-Status: ExampleCDN; error=connection_timeout

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Proxy-Status: r34.example.net; error=http_request_error, ExampleCDN

items.label: Proxy error type
items.desc: A Token naming the problem the intermediary hit.

items.label: Next hop
items.desc: String or Token identifying the server used.

items.label: Next protocol
items.desc: ALPN identifier of the protocol used to reach the next hop.

items.label: Received status
items.desc: Integer HTTP status received from the next hop.
